Title: CrowdStrike launches AI kill switch to shut down rogue agents
Context: With a notable rise in autonomous AI agents veering off-script inside corporate networks, CrowdStrike has launched an enterprise AI Kill Switch, giving security teams control to...
Full Text:
With a notable rise in autonomous AI agents veering off-script inside corporate networks, CrowdStrike has launched an enterprise AI Kill Switch, giving security teams control to cut off and disable models when they go rogue.

Integrated into its Falcon Guardian platform, this AI Kill Switch will provide security teams with the human control to terminate the agent at its root, where it runs, block it from launching again, and even cut off its enterprise network access.

The launch comes as enterprises increasingly deploy autonomous AI agents that can access sensitive data and execute tasks with limited human oversight.

“These agents can access sensitive data, execute commands and interact with business applications independently, meaning enterprises may become aware of harmful incidents only after they occur. Existing security tools protect endpoints, networks and identities but may not fully understand an agent’s instructions, reasoning, tool calls and subsequent actions,” said Soumen Mandal, principal analyst at Counterpoint Research.

Inside CrowdStrike’s AI kill switch

The AI Kill Switch has been built on Falcon Guardian, which has the capability to discover the AI agents running in the enterprise. It uses the Falcon sensor to track what an agent is instructed to do, what it communicates, and what it executes.

First, the Falcon sensor can terminate the running agent at the gateway, ensuring the malicious or misbehaving agent does not keep running while teams investigate. CrowdStrike said endpoint termination is also planned and will be available soon. Next, using the Falcon Guardian policies, the kill switch will prevent the agent from launching again on the targeted host or group of hosts. Next, it will cut-off agent’s enterprise network access.

The action can be initiated by an authorised administrator, with every action being recorded in an audit trail.

“Solutions such as CrowdStrike’s AI Kill Switch give enterprises a way to intervene quickly when AI agents behave unexpectedly, are compromised, or are manipulated through malicious instructions or scripts. This provides an important safeguard, allowing organisations to contain potentially dangerous or unauthorised agent activity before it causes significant damage,” said Devroop Dhar, MD and co-founder at Primus Partners.

However, a kill switch should be viewed as an emergency brake, not a rewind button, said Apeksha Kaushik, senior principal analyst at Gartner. She added that it may prevent additional actions, but it might not necessarily reverse all the data that has already been accessed, every system that has already been changed, all communications that have already been sent, or transactions that have already been initiated. Its effectiveness will also depend on how quickly abnormal behavior is detected, which environments are covered, and whether the agent or security infrastructure has been compromised.

An emergency brake, not a cure for AI risk

An AI Kill Switch looks promising from the details provided, but its actual effectiveness will come in after it is used extensively in live systems, warn analysts. Also, it may be a good starting point, but it cannot be viewed as a standalone solution to enterprise AI security.

“CISOs would need a more integrated approach that brings together AI discovery tools to identify unauthorised agents, runtime monitoring to track agent behaviour, robust identity and access management, and incident response and recovery mechanisms,” added Dhar.

He noted that equally important is the need for stringent AI security testing and clearly defined policies governing what agents can access and execute. There should be no ambiguity around permissions, access controls or the boundaries within which these agents are allowed to operate. The objective should be to ensure that security controls are built into the entire AI agent lifecycle rather than relying on a kill switch to intervene after something goes wrong.

Dhar added that enterprise AI agents often have access to sensitive systems, databases, applications, credentials, and APIs. A compromised or misdirected agent could therefore become a point of vulnerability. The challenge is compounded by the fact that such activity may go undetected for some time, making it difficult for organisations to identify and contain the threat.

Title: CrowdStrike to acquire Fiddler, Dreadnode to extend AI security across agent lifecycle
Context: “Enterprises should distinguish between announced plans and demonstrated product capability, with closing timeline and conditions possibly being different, especially with the...
Full Text:
CrowdStrike plans to acquire AI security companies Fiddler AI and Dreadnode in separate deals that will extend its Falcon platform into automated testing of AI systems and monitoring of AI agent behaviour, as enterprises look to address security risks arising from increasingly autonomous applications.

CrowdStrike made the announcements at Fal.Con Europe 2026 in Barcelona, saying the acquisitions will add capabilities to test AI models, applications, and agents for security weaknesses before deployment and monitor their decisions and actions in production.

The company plans to integrate Dreadnode’s automated testing technology and Fiddler’s agent observability capabilities into Falcon, with both offerings scheduled for general availability in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2027.

Dreadnode will bring automated security testing to identify vulnerabilities in AI models, applications and agents before deployment. Fiddler, meanwhile, will add AI agent observability and explainability, allowing enterprises to monitor agent behaviour, trace decisions and understand why agents take particular actions, CrowdStrike said in two separate statements.

CrowdStrike said the Dreadnode team will join its Cyber Superintelligence Lab, but did not specify how the Fiddler team would be integrated into the company.

CrowdStrike adds AI testing and observability

“With this acquisition, Dreadnode will extend the Falcon platform into the layer where enterprises build and test AI, delivering Automated AI Security Testing capabilities,” CrowdStrike said in its announcement.

It further added that Dreadnode’s technology will allow security teams to test AI models, applications, agent reasoning loops and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers against more than 100 AI attack strategies. These include jailbreaks, prompt injection, multi-turn attacks, and attacks targeting AI agents.

The technology will also let teams describe tests in natural language, rank findings by severity, and map vulnerabilities to frameworks including OWASP Top 10 for LLMs, OWASP Agentic Security, MITRE ATLAS, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework. CrowdStrike said findings will feed into Falcon Guardian as policy recommendations.

Fiddler, the second acquisition, will bring agent observability and explainability capabilities to Falcon. CrowdStrike said the technology is intended to address risks that can arise even when agents have not been compromised.

“An agent can hold valid credentials and approved tools and still make unsupported decisions, ignore instructions, or claim work it never completed. They don’t have to be compromised to create risk,” the company said in a statement.

CrowdStrike plans to offer Fiddler’s technology through Falcon Observe. The product will evaluate agent accuracy, task completion, and policy compliance before deployment, and trace decisions, reasoning paths, and tool calls once agents are in production, the company said.

The company further added that Falcon Observe will also detect behavioural drift, hallucinations and unintended actions, while maintaining records of agent activity for compliance and audit purposes. The offering is expected to support OpenTelemetry and frameworks including LangGraph, Amazon Bedrock, AWS Strands and Google ADK, it added.

Governance remains a shared responsibility

The addition of observability and automated testing to a security platform could help enterprises correlate agent behaviour with identity, runtime activity and security events, said Apeksha Kaushik, senior principal analyst at Gartner.

However, Kaushik said the acquisitions would not make security teams the sole owners of AI agent governance. Platform and observability teams would continue to be responsible for reliability, performance and operational telemetry, while application security and AI teams would retain responsibility for secure development and testing.

“Business, data and compliance leaders also retain accountability for use cases, data and regulatory obligations,” Kaushik said.

She said CIOs should establish a governance model that defines responsibilities across engineering, security, risk, and business teams. CISOs, meanwhile, should ensure security teams have the authority to set minimum controls, monitor agent behaviour and intervene when activity creates unacceptable risk.

Integration and roadmap questions

CrowdStrike expects both transactions to close during its fourth quarter of fiscal 2027, subject to customary closing conditions, and has scheduled both offerings for general availability in the same quarter.

Kaushik cautioned enterprises against treating the announced timelines as confirmation of final product capabilities or integration plans.

“Enterprises should distinguish between announced plans and demonstrated product capability, with closing timeline and conditions possibly being different, especially with the pace of change of the threat landscape and evolution of AI,” she added.

She advised customers to seek clarity on pricing, packaging, migration terms, service continuity, support commitments, deployment models, data handling, telemetry retention and API access.

“Once the Existing and prospective customers have further details, they should set up their roadmap changes, support commitments, service continuity, contract and pricing, data portability, open integrations, and access to historical data changes,” she pointed out. CrowdStrike did not disclose the financial terms of either acquisition.

Title: CrowdStrike’s AI SOC vision evolves as agentic uncertainty adds new twist
Context: Most individual components — Charlotte AI AgentWorks, Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration, the AI-enabled Enterprise Graph — were announced in 2025 as part of the company’s...
Full Text:
“The software we use has become an actor,” declared CrowdStrike President Michael Sentonas in his address on the dangers and opportunity of agentic AI at the company’s Fal.Con conference in September. It’s an idea that until recently would have been dismissed as absurd, yet across cybersecurity it’s now taken as a given.

For decades, the adversary has been nuisance hackers, professional cybercriminals, or well-resourced teams working for nation states. The arrival of rogue agents — underlined by real-world incidents such as OpenAI’s infamous assault on Hugging Face — has demolished this. Agents still work on behalf of humans, but they don’t always reason or act like them. They are entities with capabilities and an unpredictability unlike any threat businesses have ever faced.

“I believe we just crossed a line. Agents have escaped evaluation environments and compromised infrastructure they were never supposed to touch,” Sentonas told the crowd in Las Vegas in early September. “For decades, software did what we programmed it to. It has moved from execution to agency.”

Sentonas’ point wasn’t simply that malicious agents are a threat. The arrival of agentic AI also raises larger questions for security operations centers (SOCs), which will deploy agents on a scale that matches or even exceeds attackers. That makes agents a threat from both the outside and inside the enterprise perimeter. “What happens when millions of AI agents act at machine speed on both sides?” Behind the confident marketing pitches from CrowdStrike and a growing cast of rivals, the honest answer right now is that nobody can be sure.

Coming from a cyber vendor, Sentonas’ reference to “millions” of agents might sound like a number meant to hype the threat. But it is likely no exaggeration, with Gartner forecasting that the number of agents used inside a single Fortune 500 company will expand from 15 in 2025 to 150,000 by 2028.

“As CIOs and IT leaders see an explosion of AI agents across their organizations, many are contending with an ungoverned sprawl of agents that expose their organizations to a range of risks, including misinformation, oversharing, and data loss,” says Matt Goss, a senior director analyst at Gartner.

Taking up the agent challenge

For years, Fal.Con was about persuading enterprise SOCs to consolidate capabilities under CrowdStrike’s do-it-all Falcon platform, comprising nearly three dozen modules. In 2023, with its “Raptor” release, Falcon and the company’s flagship event took a hard turn toward AI. In this changed world, AI wasn’t simply a Falcon capability; increasingly it was Falcon, influencing everything it did.

The AI theme dominated Falcon’s 2026 Fall release, bringing the company’s growing portfolio of AI SOC capabilities under the Falcon umbrella with the launch of the Agentic Security Platform. Most individual components — Charlotte AI AgentWorks, Model Context Protocol (MCP) Integration, the AI-enabled Enterprise Graph — were announced in 2025 as part of the company’s Agentic Security Workforce plan but a closer look reveals important new features.

Currently, agents investigate alerts using pre-built Falcon agents or custom agents built using the no-code AgentWorks solution. Charlotte AI now gives these agents a shared memory layer in Enterprise Graph that enables them to coordinate with one another across multiple endpoints, identities, and cloud services simultaneously (aided by the company’s 2025 acquisition of Onum, which accelerated the speed with which agents can ingest data). On paper, the effect is to dramatically speed up alert triage while expanding the scope and capacity of worker agents in a way that relieves human SOC teams of a lot of basic grunt work, including some Level 2 investigation and Level 3 remediation and hunting workflows.

Also new is SafeMind, a frontier red-teaming system based on Nvidia’s Nemotron open-weight LLM, comprising offense (Red Tempest) and defense (Blue Solano). This agentic framework continuously tests an isolated mirror of the live environment for weaknesses, feeding the results back into detection at the agent level. CrowdStrike didn’t invent the concept, but it does appear to be the first to integrate an autonomous testing model into a SOC platform.

Speed is not enough

This might look brand new, but the early incarnations of the agent-powered SOC are as much evolution as revolution. Everything inside a traditional CrowdStrike-powered SOC — from its Falcon EDR sensor, Enterprise Graph data, and cloud-native management — remains in place. Humans are still essential to decision-making, albeit at a higher level than before. What agents add to this SOC paradigm is a new abstraction layer separating SOC teams from the mass of telemetry they have increasingly struggled with. This should be good news for defenders because it means they have some hope of matching the speed and scale of agentic attacks.

But speed is only the beginning, points out James Patrick, CTO for the FIOR Group, which develops an AI policy and security gateway. “Attackers and defenders can both operate at machine speed, so simply making SOCs faster isn’t enough. We need to move beyond reactive detection towards continuous testing of our defenses.”

SOCs must work out how much they delegate to agents and what constraints are set around this. “Enterprises already struggle with fragmented telemetry, overlapping security products and inconsistent policies. Adding autonomous systems introduces another problem: establishing who or what has authority to act, and how to verify that authority,” says Patrick.

According to Chris Cochran, field CISO and VP of AI security for the SANS Institute, that’s why “for most organizations, agentic AI will be augmentative rather than a replacement for analysts, at least for the next few years.”

Agent platforms, including CrowdStrike’s, still have work to do proving themselves in terms of oversight and governance.

“The core problem is that we’re applying a probabilistic technology to a discipline that usually requires determinism,” Cochran adds. “A SOC needs to know that the same input will produce the same action, and that the action can be explained to an auditor or an incident review board.”

For that reason, Cochran believes that while agentic-powered SOCs will remove a huge amount of alert handling and correlation effort, the workload will shift to processes such as verification.

“Teams should continuously evaluate agents against known-good and known-bad cases, the same way you’d regression test detection content,” he says. “None of this is exotic, but it takes engineering time that many SOCs haven’t budgeted for.”

Enemy within

One deeply unfamiliar problem is that agents themselves are an emerging attack surface within the enterprise and must be constantly assessed. Traditionally, security tools defend the environment, and the idea that an agent system doing the same job could itself become a direct threat is new. But what makes agentic AI unsettlingly is its non-deterministic nature, which means that, unlike a traditional security tool, it has the potential to do things you didn’t tell it to and haven’t planned for.

“Organizations are deploying autonomous systems that access sensitive data, use privileged identities, interact with applications, and execute actions. Those agents can be compromised, manipulated, or behave unexpectedly,” says Tom Findling, CEO and cofounder at AI SOC startup Conifers.ai. “Security operations will need visibility into agent identities, permissions, actions, and decision-making processes, and the ability to detect and contain dangerous behavior.”

CrowdStrike’s answer, relaunched at this year’s Fal.Con, is Falcon Guardian, an AI detection and response (AIDR) solution featuring runtime enforcement, agent discovery, execution graph mapping prompts, and quarantining for misbehaving agents. Similar capabilities will be needed for any agent platform but the mere fact that security systems now need their own security systems underscores what CrowdStrike’s Sentonas was referring to with his software-as-actor remark at Fal.Con. Human SOCs need to protect their enterprises from their AI SOC helpers.

To that end, CrowdStrike yesterday announced the roughly $400 million acquisition of Fiddler AI, an AI agent monitoring and governance vendor from the emerging, burgeoning, and somewhat confusing agentic AI tools ecosystem.

Fiddler’s platform tracks AI models’ behavior, attempting to provide explanations for their actions as a means for establishing a control plane for governing and securing them. Its 100-plus metrics track hallucinations, toxicity, personally identifiable information (PII) leakage, and drift, enforcing policies to protect against jailbreaks, prompt injections, and bias. Enterprises deploy tools like Fiddler to make model drift visible and actionable before it becomes systemic risk.

CrowdStrike intends to bundle Fiddler into its flagship platform as Falcon Observe in Q4 FY2027, approximately six months from now, as a means for “proving businesses can safely use AI agents every day,” according to Sentonas’ post announcing the acquisition.

CrowdStrike has invested heavily in agentic AI, building an impressive stack of capabilities that extend the Enterprise Graph that made it a dominant player capable of surviving the occasional embarrassing global hiccup. It has even embraced a degree of openness, allowing data ingestion, API connectors, and partnership gateways to enrich the data going into its Falcon AIDR. However, there’s no getting away from Falcon as the single control plane.

“CrowdStrike starts with endpoint security and an established enterprise security platform. Other vendors approach the problem through identity, networks, cloud, or security analytics. They all have an incentive to bring customers further into their own platforms,” observes FIOR Group’s Patrick.

“The challenge for CrowdStrike, and for every vendor, is that a platform can’t independently verify itself,” he adds. “What’s needed is control that is genuinely independent of any single platform and works across those boundaries.”

According to Patrick, a critical feature will be the ability not simply to deploy a security layer but to continuously assess its security and performance. As the traditional detection and remediation stack of cybersecurity is pushed out of shape, the growth in new layers and processes could make this task almost as demanding as the main job of cyber defense that agents were supposed to simplify.

Title: CrowdStrike Extends the Agentic SOC to Detect and Stop Agent Insider Threats
Context: This foundation extends to the place many of these attacks begin: the AI tooling agents depend on
Full Text:
When individual signals are brought together, a clear picture forms. With Dynamic Risk Scoring (Q4), agent risk feeds into the same 0 to 100 risk score that Falcon Next-Gen SIEM already builds for the agent's owner and host. When an agent, its user, and its device all climb the risk list together, the coordination behind otherwise routine activity is harder to miss.

This foundation extends to the place many of these attacks begin: the AI tooling agents depend on. AI Ecosystem Detections (Q4) add detection logic for attacks on AI services, including LLM API abuse, stolen API keys, and the compromise of coding assistants, MCP servers, and agent frameworks. When the threat starts in a trusted tool rather than the agent itself, the Falcon platform is watching there too.

Because the context around an agent doesn't always live inside the Falcon platform, Federated Search Expansion lets teams search related data where it already lives, without re-ingestion. New connectors for GovCloud, Dynatrace, Databricks, and Snowflake are now generally available, with Splunk, Elastic, and Cribl Lake connectors following in Q4.

Act on Tough Questions

Once a risky agent surfaces, every analyst faces the same question: Did an agent’s owner do this, or did their agent do it without them knowing?

This is the work Multi-Agent Triage and Investigation (GA, announced at Fal.Con US 2026) was built for. SOC agents investigate detections end to end, with specialist agents working the case together on shared context across endpoint, identity, and the agent's activity.

Investigation coverage already spans the full range of Falcon platform and third-party sources. In Q4, triage coverage extends to CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian, CrowdStrike Falcon® Cloud Security, CrowdStrike Falcon® Shield, CrowdStrike Falcon® Data Security, and custom detections, including abnormal agent behavior flagged by Falcon Next-Gen SIEM. When an agent is flagged, it routes straight into an agentic investigation where the agent, its owner, and its host are already connected.

This shared context is what answers the tough question. Investigating agents can trace a session back to what the person asked for and separate it from what the agent did on its own. When the person's request was routine and everything that followed traces to instructions they never wrote, the verdict becomes clear: The insider was the agent, not the employee.

But a verdict doesn't stop a compromised agent that's still running. The Unified Agentic SOAR Experience (GA, announced at Fal.Con US 2026) is where response happens. Teams build, run, and govern all automation in the SOC, from AI agents to workflows to custom apps, in plain language. They set the mission and define triggers, data, rules, and actions to decide what runs autonomously and what requires approval. A single response decision can coordinate everything that needs to follow in parallel: stopping the agent, cutting off its access, keeping it from coming back, and documenting what happened. It's open by design and connects to any agent, model, or tool through API or MCP, so teams can govern automation across the security stack with visibility into what it's costing and what needs attention.

See it in action:

Autonomy That Earns Its Trust

As SOCs hand more of the work to agents, the controls that keep agents accountable matter as much as the speed they deliver.

CrowdStrike builds governance into every layer of the agentic SOC. It starts by watching the SOC's agents. Policy-Drift Agent Guardrails, powered by Falcon Guardian (Beta, Q4), screen every CrowdStrike Charlotte AI™ and AgentWorks interaction for policy drift, unauthorized tool calls, and out-of-bounds data access to catch the moment an agent steps outside its intended scope.

Title: CrowdStrike Introduces Agentic Adversary Emulation to Counter AI-Enabled Adversaries
Context: Attack Path Discovery to Validated Defense Reveal Potential Attack Paths Instead of simply identifying vulnerabilities, Agentic Adversary Emulation shows how attackers could...
Full Text:
Frontier AI is enabling threat actors to rapidly learn an environment, identify weaknesses, and chain them into viable paths to critical systems. These capabilities allow adversaries to move faster while exploiting vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and other gaps to achieve their goals.

Traditional exposure management helps organizations identify and prioritize weaknesses largely as individual risks, and periodic red team engagements only provide deeper validation at a point in time. Neither approach alone can continuously validate defenses at the speed and scale of AI-enabled adversaries. Organizations must understand not only where they are exposed, but what adversaries could achieve and whether corrective actions can strengthen their defenses.

To fight AI-enabled adversaries with AI, CrowdStrike is introducing Agentic Adversary Emulation, a new AI-powered red teaming capability powered by CrowdStrike® SafeMind. It’s now in early access.

Agentic Adversary Emulation combines specialized AI models and offensive harnesses with real-world adversary intelligence and deep knowledge of customer environments. Operating within controlled, customer-approved boundaries in production environments, it uncovers exploitable attack paths, generates prioritized remediation recommendations and compensating controls, and validates whether corrective actions have strengthened defenses.

Attack Path Discovery to Validated Defense

Reveal Potential Attack Paths

Instead of simply identifying vulnerabilities, Agentic Adversary Emulation shows how attackers could exploit and chain weaknesses across systems and identities to compromise critical assets, and where defenses can stop them. This helps security teams understand what attackers could accomplish in their environment.

Turn Findings into Defensive Action

Agentic Adversary Emulation translates these exploitable attack paths into prioritized remediation actions and compensating controls that security teams can review and deploy through the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform. These may include applying patches, changing configurations, updating security policies, and creating new detections. By connecting demonstrated attack paths to corrective actions, this helps organizations focus on the weaknesses attackers can exploit and take targeted action to disrupt their progress.

Verify that Fixes Work

After corrective actions are implemented, Agentic Adversary Emulation repeats the attack simulation to verify whether those changes successfully disrupt previously identified attack paths. This helps organizations determine whether their fixes work and whether security controls can prevent adversaries from advancing toward critical assets. By connecting attack path discovery, remediation, and validation, Agentic Adversary Emulation creates a closed loop across offense and defense: attack, defend, and validate.

The CrowdStrike Advantage in AI-Powered Red Teaming

Agentic Adversary Emulation combines three core CrowdStrike capabilities to bring real-world adversary behavior into AI-powered red team testing:

Industry-leading adversary intelligence: CrowdStrike pioneered adversary-driven threat intelligence and tracks more than 290 adversaries globally. Recognized as a Leader by both Gartner and Forrester in threat intelligence, CrowdStrike draws on frontline threat hunting, incident response, CrowdStrike Falcon® platform telemetry, and intelligence on emerging threats to bring the latest adversary tradecraft directly into red team testing.

Deep knowledge of customer environments: The Falcon platform provides rich context across assets, identities, vulnerabilities, configurations, and security controls. This enables CrowdStrike to go beyond generic attack scenarios to emulate how adversaries could exploit interconnected weaknesses in a customer's environment to gain access to critical systems.

Powered by CrowdStrike SafeMind: SafeMind provides the purpose-built AI models and offensive harnesses that drive Agentic Adversary Emulation. Combining CrowdStrike’s latest adversary intelligence with deep visibility into customer environments, these systems emulate real-world adversary behavior at machine speed, continuously exploring attack paths and adapting as new weaknesses are discovered. Operating within customer-approved boundaries, they identify exploitable weaknesses, reveal how attackers could chain them together, and demonstrate what adversaries could achieve against critical assets.

During early access, CrowdStrike will work closely with selected customers to conduct controlled red teaming within defined safeguards and customer-approved boundaries, while refining the operational guardrails for safe execution in production environments.

Bringing Threat Intelligence to Smartphones

As AI accelerates adversary operations, security teams need trusted intelligence to make faster decisions, wherever they are. CrowdStrike is bringing its industry-leading threat intelligence and agentic AI capabilities to a new mobile app for iOS and Android. Available to CrowdStrike Falcon® Adversary Intelligence Premium customers, the app extends the Falcon experience beyond the desktop, providing direct access to the latest intelligence reports and the Threat Intelligence Agent.

Through the new app, customers can:

Stay ahead of emerging threats: Access expert-validated intelligence on adversaries, including their latest activities, evolving tactics, and emerging campaigns, to understand threats as they develop.

Act faster: Ask the Threat Intelligence Agent questions in natural language to quickly understand adversaries, campaigns, vulnerabilities, and emerging threats, identify what matters most, and determine what actions to take.

Make informed decisions anywhere: Access trusted intelligence and AI-driven analysis wherever decisions need to be made, without being tied to a desktop or the Falcon console.

Advancing Adversary-Driven Security for the AI Era

With Agentic Adversary Emulation and the new threat intelligence mobile app, CrowdStrike is expanding how organizations put adversary intelligence to work, from proactively simulating attacks and strengthening defenses to making informed security decisions wherever they are. Together, these innovations help defenders stay ahead of evolving threats through faster, more proactive, intelligence-driven security.

Title: CrowdStrike Brings Enterprise Browser Security to the Falcon Platform
Context: The browser has become a critical enterprise attack surface
Full Text:
The browser has become a critical enterprise attack surface. Employees rely on the browser to access business applications, interact with AI tools, and handle sensitive data. Knowing this, attackers seek to exploit browser sessions for credential theft and data exfiltration.

Today, CrowdStrike Falcon® Seraphic® Enterprise Browser is natively available on the CrowdStrike Falcon platform, extending protection into the browser. Security teams can manage browser security alongside existing Falcon capabilities through a unified platform experience. This provides a simpler way to protect browser activity across managed and unmanaged devices, without requiring employees to adopt a dedicated enterprise browser or reroute traffic.

The availability of Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser on the Falcon platform delivers three key advantages:

Less to manage: Browser security, secure remote access, and BYOD/contractor access are managed directly within the organization’s Falcon platform environment.

Faster to deploy: Protection works in the browsers teams already use; there is no need to deploy a dedicated browser or reroute traffic.

Coverage where the sensor can't go: Protection extends to unmanaged, BYOD, and contractor devices without mobile device management (MDM) enrollment.

Stop Browser-Based Threats, Protect Data, and Secure Access

Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser provides real-time security controls inside browser sessions, where users access applications, handle sensitive data, and interact with AI tools. Its browser-layer capabilities address five important use cases:

Blocking browser-based attacks: Runtime inspection helps detect and disrupt malicious browser activity, including phishing, ClickFix, malicious scripts, and adversary-in-the-middle attacks.

Identity and session protection: Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser extends protection beyond authentication to help stop session token theft and session hijacking within active browser sessions.

Data and AI controls at the point of use: Teams can enforce policies on browser actions such as copy, paste, upload, and download; this helps prevent sensitive data from reaching unsanctioned web applications and generative AI tools.

Browser extension management: Security teams can inventory browser extensions, evaluate their risk, and enforce policies that allow or block risky extensions across supported browsers.

Secure access to private applications: Policy-controlled access to internal web applications and resources is provided for employees and contractors, including on unmanaged devices, without relying on traditional VPN or VDI for supported workflows.

Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser complements the broader security context of the Falcon platform. With browser telemetry available in CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM, analysts can search, investigate, and correlate browser activity with endpoint, identity, and third-party data to accelerate triage and response. With richer context and more places to act, security teams can follow the adversary rather than the boundaries between products.

Built for How Teams Work

As enterprise work increasingly happens in browsers, SaaS applications, and AI tools, browser security can no longer operate in isolation. By bringing Falcon Seraphic Enterprise Browser into the Falcon platform, CrowdStrike extends protection into the browser while unifying security operations across more of the enterprise attack surface. This helps organizations stop threats, protect sensitive data, and reduce operational complexity.

Title: New Falcon Cloud Security Innovations Secure the Cloud AI Runs On
Context: New detections combining Cloud Indicators of Attack (IOAs) with posture insights bring exposure context directly into threat detection
Full Text:
AI is accelerating both sides of cloud security. Developers and coding agents are writing more code, pulling in more open source packages, and launching more cloud and AI workloads than security teams can review by hand. Adversaries use AI to move faster, and they are targeting everything organizations build and run, from the packages in automated pipelines, to the identities that control cloud resources, to the infrastructure powering AI applications.

Security teams must keep pace on both fronts to defend against this acceleration and secure the cloud their AI runs on. CrowdStrike Falcon® Cloud Security is built for this. It is powered by adversary intelligence tracking 290+ adversaries, so detections and risk prioritization reflect how attackers operate in the cloud. It runs on the same CrowdStrike Falcon platform that connects endpoint and identity protection with SOC operations, extending protection from developer endpoints and software supply chains to cloud workloads. Because proactive security and real-time cloud detection and response (CDR) share one platform, the exposure and attack path context teams build before an attack becomes the context analysts use to stop one.

The latest Falcon Cloud Security innovations, all now generally available, put this advantage to work from build to runtime. They help organizations stop compromised software before production, protect AI workloads and the infrastructure supporting them, and detect cloud attacks in seconds. Proactive security informs runtime defense by giving teams the context to understand risks and when to act on them. This connected defense spans business and mission-critical environments, including some of the hardest to secure.

Reduce Risk and Stop Threats Before Production

Securing the cloud that AI runs on starts with understanding where organizations are exposed and whether software entering production can be trusted. Falcon Cloud Security connects cloud risk, application context, and adversary intelligence to help teams close exposures before software is deployed.

Stop Supply Chain Threats

AI coding agents are pulling open source packages into automated builds faster than teams can review them. Adversaries can exploit that trust by compromising otherwise legitimate software. CrowdStrike observed ALTERED SPIDER compromise more than 300 software dependencies in a single day.1 A compromised dependency does not need a CVE to be dangerous, which means vulnerability scanning alone can miss the threat.

Supply Chain Security for Cloud extends the adversary intelligence CrowdStrike uses to detect and quarantine malicious packages on endpoints into container images. Falcon Cloud Security identifies compromised npm and PyPI packages during CI/CD and registry scanning, automatically reassesses previously scanned images as new threats are confirmed, and identifies affected running containers.

At deployment, the Falcon Kubernetes Admission Controller uses image assessment policies to alert on or block compromised images before they reach production. Together, endpoint and cloud protection connect the defense from package download through deployment to help teams stop compromised software.

Expand Cloud Risk and Asset Visibility

Security teams need to understand how exposures combine into opportunities for an adversary. Full Text:
AI agents are transforming enterprise computing. What began with employees using AI assistants is evolving into autonomous agents that access enterprise resources, invoke tools, execute code, and take action at machine speed.

This introduces a new security and safety challenge. Organizations must protect agents from attacks while ensuring those agents operate safely and as intended. Security teams need to discover where agents operate, understand what they were instructed to do, trace their actions, and intervene when their behavior becomes dangerous.

Traditional security approaches provide only part of the picture. Endpoint runtime security monitors execution but lacks the AI-specific context needed to explain what triggered it. Network inspection can monitor AI communications but not the actions that agents take on systems. Agent-level integrations can inspect AI interactions but cannot reveal downstream execution.

At Fal.Con Europe 2026, CrowdStrike unveiled innovations that advance AI detection and response (AIDR) across three critical dimensions: architecture, coverage, and controls. We also introduced a new AI kill switch for CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian that empowers security teams to rapidly cut off AI model access at AI gateways when agents become dangerous. And we shared the general availability of CrowdStrike Falcon® Complete for Guardian, which extends 24/7 managed detection and response to AI security.

The Right Architecture for Securing AI Agents

Securing AI agents requires visibility and control across three critical layers: OS-level runtime execution, network communications, and agent interactions. Falcon Guardian brings these layers together to connect what agents are instructed to do with what they execute.

OS-level runtime security is the foundation (Available now): The Falcon sensor provides deep visibility into agents’ activity, including the processes they launch, commands they run, and resources they access. This visibility is not achievable directly via network inspection or per-agent hook integration approaches.

Endpoint network inspection extends visibility into agent communications (Pre-beta): CrowdStrike announced plans to expand this capability to macOS, where it will inspect traffic entering and leaving the endpoint to help security teams identify risky interactions.

Agent-level hooks provide direct inspection and policy enforcement within supported AI agents (Available now): Hooks for Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, and Cursor enable organizations to inspect prompts and block malicious activity at the source, before harmful actions are executed.

Together, these three layers give Falcon Guardian visibility into agent instructions, communications, and runtime execution. CrowdStrike® Agent Graph connects this activity, linking what agents were instructed to do with what they actually executed and the resources they affected. This gives security teams the context to understand agent behavior, investigate threats, and trace their impact from prompt to process.

See it in action:

The Right Coverage: Secured AI Wherever It Operates

Falcon Guardian initially focused on securing workforce AI adoption and autonomous agents at the endpoint, where employees interact with AI and agents execute with user permissions.

Now, as enterprises build and deploy their own agents in production environments, CrowdStrike is expanding Falcon Guardian's AI-specific protections across more of the cloud infrastructure the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform already secures. Newly announced capabilities will extend Falcon Guardian coverage across Linux, cloud workloads, Kubernetes, and managed AI platforms.

Expanded cloud coverage (Pre-beta): On Linux, Falcon Guardian will bring agent discovery, visibility, and AI-specific detections to Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. In cloud workloads and Kubernetes, Falcon Guardian will extend these capabilities to enterprise-developed AI agents and applications, including those built with LangChain and LangGraph. Using the Falcon Linux sensor, deployed directly or as a Kubernetes DaemonSet, Falcon Guardian will connect AI activity with surrounding runtime, workload, and identity context.

For provider-managed AI environments, Falcon Guardian will expand agent discovery and AI-layer visibility, beginning with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. This will help security teams identify managed agents, understand their components and interactions, and assess AI-specific risks without requiring access to provider-controlled infrastructure.

Context: Built in partnership with Anthropic in response to enterprise customer demand, this integration extends Falcon protection to AI agents across their lifecycle, from agent...
Full Text:
When Claude Cowork executes code locally, it runs inside an isolated virtual machine on the user's computer. On the host, that VM runs as a single opaque process: The agent's activity inside the VM, including the processes it spawns, the packages it installs, and the network connections it makes, is not visible to the host's endpoint security sensor. Because host folders can be mounted into the VM, sensitive data can sit within the agent's reach.

Today at Fal.Con Europe 2026, CrowdStrike announced it is bringing CrowdStrike Falcon® Guardian protection natively into Anthropic's Claude Cowork. Built in partnership with Anthropic in response to enterprise customer demand, this integration extends Falcon protection to AI agents across their lifecycle, from agent creation through job execution. It runs the Falcon sensor directly inside the Cowork VM on both macOS and Windows to bring runtime visibility and detection into the agent's execution environment.

The integration is now available in beta on macOS, with Windows support expected later in November.

How It Works

Consider this scenario: A user asks Cowork for a script to align their slides to a brand standard. While completing the task, the agent installs the latest version of a common Python package. Neither the user nor the agent knows that an adversary has compromised the package at its source. Once installed, that package reads host data through a mounted folder and sends it out to a known malicious endpoint. The Falcon sensor running inside the VM would detect it. This is exactly the type of malicious activity and potential data exfiltration the integration is built to detect as agents execute tasks.

CrowdStrike’s sensor integration with the Cowork VM will deliver:

Visibility and detection where agents execute: Process, package, and network activity inside the Cowork VM will no longer be a blind spot, so teams can detect and investigate threats with the same Falcon telemetry they use everywhere else.

The same visibility on macOS and Windows: The VM runs the same Linux environment on both, so customers get consistent coverage regardless of the OS.

Deployment and control through the CrowdStrike Falcon® platform: Admins will turn the integration on through their existing device management, the same way they deploy the Falcon sensor today, and the Falcon Linux sensor deploys inside the Cowork VM. From there, the team controls it through the Falcon platform so Claude Cowork comes under the same security control plane as the rest of the environment.

Built with Anthropic

CrowdStrike and Anthropic worked together to bring Falcon protection directly into Claude Cowork's execution environment. Anthropic enabled Falcon deployment within Cowork, while CrowdStrike engineered and tested the integration across installation, real-time protection, and ongoing updates. Through this beta integration, enterprises can extend the security they already trust from the Falcon platform to AI agents in Claude Cowork, alongside the virtual machine, permissions, and admin controls built into Cowork.

CrowdStrike’s Architectural Difference

AI agents don't operate in one layer, and neither does Falcon Guardian. Agents reach out over the network to communicate with LLMs, but they also execute processes locally on the workstations where they’re installed. These actions may never cross network boundaries. The Falcon sensor and Falcon Guardian see both agentic workstreams and fuse them together in a single view from CrowdStrike’s endpoint network inspection and OS-level visibility. This unified view, CrowdStrike® Agent Graph, shows analysts not only what agents were asked to do, but what they did at runtime.

CrowdStrike also delivers agent-level enforcement controls via hook integrations for agents such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, OpenCode, and Cursor.

The Claude Cowork integration extends Falcon Guardian coverage to a new place agents work. It takes Falcon Guardian’s runtime security foundation into the VM where Cowork runs its code, providing visibility and detection for what the agent executes, installs, and connects to across its lifecycle, from agent creation through job execution.

What's Next

Endpoint agents like Claude Cowork run their code inside a VM that host-only security can't see into. By running the Falcon Linux sensor inside the Cowork VM on macOS and Windows, this integration will close that gap. It will bring Falcon visibility and detection to where agents execute, it will be deployed and controlled through Falcon, and it will extend the runtime foundation of the three layers of AI security in Falcon Guardian.

The integration is focused on visibility and detection inside the VM. Available in beta on macOS, with Windows support expected later in November 2026, it enables customers to deploy the Falcon Linux sensor inside the Cowork VM through their existing device management tools. Their teams gain visibility and detection across the processes, packages, and network activity inside the VM.

Title: What Makes a Good Security Agent? 5 Lessons from the AgentWorks Hackathon
Context: Working with NVIDIA, we launched the first AgentWorks Hackathon and invited security teams to nominate agents they’ve built
Full Text:
Every security team is being told to adopt AI. Far fewer have been shown what "good" looks like in practice. Turnkey agents handle common, well-defined security tasks, but no two security teams operate the same way. Each has its own data, playbooks, escalation paths, and risk tolerances; unique context that no vendor can anticipate in a packaged solution. That’s why we built CrowdStrike® Charlotte AI™ AgentWorks: a no-code workspace that lets every security team build the exact agents they need, on the Falcon platform.

The power of the crowd is one of the most enduring advantages we have as an industry against the adversary. What one analyst learns on the front lines, the whole community inherits. Now, adversaries are rapidly gaining AI fluency, and defenders need to transform the SOC the way we always have: together. When one team turns a hard problem into a working agent, it raises the bar for all of us. Every team can learn from that agent, adapt it, and build on it.

So, we summoned the ingenuity of the crowd like never before. Working with NVIDIA, we launched the first AgentWorks Hackathon and invited security teams to nominate agents they’ve built. The brief was wide open: each team picked its own problem and defined its build. Nearly a hundred nominations poured in from more than 50 countries, each aimed at a persistent bottleneck its builders knew firsthand and forged to earn its place as a trusted extension of the team.

The standouts went further. They were intentionally designed, governed by clear guardrails, and deliver real impact. Here are the winning agents and five lessons every security team can apply today.

Winner Spotlights

“Agent Smith”: Finding the MCP Servers Nobody Knew Were Running

AI coding tools can launch an MCP server on a developer laptop with a single command. Most security teams have no inventory of them. In one day, one company discovered 1,710 hosts running unapproved MCP servers, including a revoked server, unapproved mailbox readers, and one with TLS verification turned off. Nobody had been watching.

Agent Smith hunts these cases down. It finds MCP servers running on endpoints, checks each against the organization's approved list, and reads redacted command lines for risky settings. In doing so, it turns a blind spot into a daily inventory with a clear next step for every server.

The sophistication here wasn't just in the prompt. It was in the architecture: a deliberate division of labor between the model and deterministic tools like queries and workflows. That split sharpened accuracy and controlled cost.

Before the agent runs, an upstream query in CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM does the heavy lifting, carrying the company's own context: signature rules encoding the approved tool list, noise filters tuned during testing, and host lookups mapping each server to a business unit. It also redacts sensitive data before handing the agent a command-line sample and package names.

The agent then gets to work: explaining what each server is, flagging risky settings (TLS off, unpinned versions, credentials on the command line), and recommending a next step based on the team's existing approval process (switch to an approved server, request a review, or register a custom build). Charlotte Agentic SOAR then passes that context into a new case for the governance team to review.

“Help Desk Takeover Defender” Agent: Catching MFA Reset Abuse in 70 Seconds

Multifactor authentication (MFA) exploitation is one of the most effective plays in the modern attacker's playbook: Call the service desk, impersonate an employee, get their MFA reset, register your own device, and walk into the account. The challenge for defenders is that a malicious reset can look almost exactly like a legitimate one.

The Help Desk Takeover Defender agent ensures every MFA reset is investigated for abuse within moments of a new reset. Manual investigations that previously took 20 to 30 minutes now run in about 70 seconds against live data, and containment drops from hours to minutes. It pulls Entra ID logs and the supporting Falcon telemetry behind a reset, then scores the likelihood of a social engineering attack. If the signs point to a takeover, it can revoke sessions, disable the user, or contain the host.

What earned this agent its recognition was how it balanced trust and speed. The scoring is deterministic, computed upstream by a CrowdStrike Falcon® Foundry function rather than the model, so the same evidence produces the same verdict. The model compares each reset against that user's 30-day history, then draws on knowledge files that encode the team's playbook: what's considered normal, how to verify a user with a callback, and which containment paths are warranted and when. No action happens without a human in the loop: Every containment step requires explicit approval and the approver's name on record.

“Exclusion Adversary” Agent: The Agent that Attacks its Own Work

Every security team manages exclusions: rules that tell security tools to stop alerting on recurring, harmless activity. But left unattended, exclusions can become blind spots of their own. A rule written too loosely doesn't just quiet the noise; it hides any real attack that happens to share the same pattern. A good exclusion has to thread the needle: wide enough to catch the noise, but tight enough that an attacker can't hide behind it.

The Exclusion Adversary agent turns that balancing act into a repeatable, evidence-backed step. It gathers live detection counts and drafts the narrowest exclusion that would safely apply. Then it does what analysts rarely have time for: It attacks its own draft. It lists every field the rule leaves wide open and writes bypass strings an adversary might use to slip through, such as a same-named binary dropped in a writable folder. It ends with a verdict and an approval checklist for an analyst to review.

What sets this agent apart is its adversarial mindset turned inward. Most agents try to be right. This one assumes it might be wrong and goes looking for proof. Its discipline caught a real defect in testing: The agent's first draft used a common wildcard pattern that matched a program by name in any folder. That meant an attacker could plant a lookalike elsewhere and the exclusion would silence it too. The agent flagged the gap and tightened the rule to the exact file path.

Notable Runners-Up

This is CQL Agent: Security queries can run without errors but still fail. AI-drafted detections are especially prone to this. This agent checks whether queries and detection rules work as intended. It takes output from CrowdStrike’s LogScale query assistant or the Falcon Next-Gen SIEM Correlation Rule Generation Agent and runs it through a fixed series of gates, including a check against a 196-function CrowdStrike Query Language (CQL) catalog, 23 silent-failure rules, and a reproducible unit test. Each one ends with a verdict: validated, validated with limits, or inconclusive. Judges singled out its reproducible tests and its willingness to return an inconclusive result. An agent that admits what it can't prove is one you can trust when it returns a "validated” verdict.

TaHiTI Threat Hunting Agent: Structured threat hunting can take a senior analyst hours; most of it spent on research, schema lookups, query debugging, and write-ups rather than hunting. This agent runs the full Targeted Hunting integrating Threat Intelligence (TaHiTI) methodology end-to-end. It scopes queries to keep costs under control and produces a standardized, ServiceNow-ready hunt record. The result: junior analysts can now run hunts that once waited on senior staff. The method stops living in one person's head and can be run by the whole team.

HOPSCOTCH Agent (Lateral Movement Flight Recorder): Tracing an identity or process across entry, internal hops, and exit points can be a time-consuming process. Given an account name, HOPSCOTCH reconstructs that entity’s path as a chronological, confidence-rated chain, corroborating source activity, authentication, destination execution, and post-arrival behavior at each hop. At each link, the agent provides supporting evidence and a confidence level, so analysts can see what it knows and what it’s inferring.

EASM Heartbeat Agent: An organization's external attack surface changes constantly. Each morning, the EASM Heartbeat agent emails the security team a short report on what changed across its external attack surface in the last 24 hours: new findings, new IPs, new “Critical” and “High” CVE misconfigurations, and which way the risk score is moving. One weekend, its findings more than doubled, tracing the spike to newly attributed assets carrying critical, actively used exploits. Its report revealed to the team that much of the inventory had never been reviewed, which led to a recurring asset review.

Dysfunctional Family-Tree Agent: Most attacks today are malware-free. To catch them, this agent proactively audits two- and three-generation process lineage (grandparent, parent, child) against a lookup table of patterns common to LOLBin attacks, decodes obfuscated command lines, and opens a case for medium-or-worse findings.

Hall Pass Agent: Security exemptions rarely expire on their own. One organization found more than 25,000 hosts carrying a USB exemption, with no active approval on record for over two years. The Hall Pass agent reconciles the exemptions the Falcon platform enforces against internal approval records, measures whether each is still used, and opens a renew-or-revoke case for the owner, so exceptions stay current and reviewed.

SneakerNet Agent: The Falcon sensor records every file written to USB, far too many for any team to review by hand. In a 30 day window, one team found merger documents, litigation holds, and pay statements copied to removable drives without triggering a single alert. Blocking USB would break legitimate work, so every hour a detection query flags sensitive files written to or opened from USB drives and SD cards. The agent scores each device, checking the machine’s role and whether the same drive has been on other hosts. It then opens a case for the data owner showing what left, how, and why it scored the way it did, without blocking anything or naming the user.

What Makes a Good Security Agent?

Five traits set apart the best agents:

They solve real problems: The best agents target the work that drains analyst time, or worse, the work that always loses to urgent tasks and never gets done. These problems aren't always glamorous, but they're often low-risk and high-return cases for automation. Moreover, the best builds didn't just move a bottleneck downstream or create new ones. They closed the gap, doing work that otherwise wouldn't happen.

They connect data, reasoning, and action, and plug into processes that teams already run: A good agent is defined by an architecture that applies AI reasoning exactly where judgment is needed and leans on other technologies for everything else. The strongest builds didn't make the model do everything. They made it do the one thing only a model can, then handed the rest to tools that are faster, cheaper, and deterministic, such as for routing, loops, query searches, and fixed calculations. They also structured outputs to hand off cleanly to the workflows, cases, and agents downstream.

They have built-in guardrails: The best builders treated trust as a design problem. They capped tool calls, retry limits, and per-run credits. They redacted sensitive data before the model ever saw it. They refused to let the model invent facts, or required a named human to approve any consequential action. The best of them made the dangerous action structurally impossible, such as instructing agents to disclose when information is incomplete or routing containment through workflows that require analyst approval. As one judge noted, “For a cyberdefense team, an agent’s ability to disclose missing evidence, avoid unsupported conclusions, and preserve human control matters as much as its speed.”

They drive measurable outcomes and improve over time: The top builds were designed around tasks that could be evaluated, then refined across versions and benchmarked against real or synthetic datasets until they met the required bar for accuracy. This is what separates a demo from a production-ready agent: one that can be measured and continuously optimized, earning the trust to graduate to more autonomous work.

They're creative: Some of the most memorable submissions weren't faster versions of existing work. They approached problems from entirely new angles: an agent that attacks detection exclusions to expose the blind spot, an agent that hunts down unauthorized agents. Some of the most forward-looking builds pointed at questions the industry is only beginning to ask, like whether an agent's activity isn’t just internally authorized but legal under local regulations.

Agent Traces: How the Best Agents Got Even Better

One last habit set the standout agents apart: They used AgentWorks agent traces to understand how their agent worked and to optimize its design.

Every time an AgentWorks agent runs, it leaves an execution trace, a step-by-step record of what the agent did: which tools it called, the exact query it sent, what came back, how long each step took, and how many credits each step consumed. The trace view is a powerful resource for troubleshooting and optimizing agent design. Builders noted how this helped them troubleshoot four common issues:

Errors the agent ignores: A tool errors out, and the agent either moves on or quietly substitutes different results, building a confident conclusion on missing data. The fix: Include explicit prompt instructions for how to handle errors, including never filling gaps with substitute data.

Zero rows misread as "none": No error appears, just an empty result. The agent reports "nothing found" when the real cause was a timeout or a query that never ran. The fix: Have the agent confirm the query completed before reporting "none," and report "not retrieved" if it can't. Then redesign the query, for example by narrowing the time window, rather than retrying it unchanged.

Over-chaining and wasted turns: Timeouts and excessive agent-to-agent chaining inflate latency and cost without improving accuracy. The fix: Trim the chain to the steps that actually improve the answer, and remove tools the agent doesn't need.

Knowledge bases that never got used: An agent is only as good as its context. Traces can also reveal when agents don’t open their attached knowledge base. The fix: Force a knowledge lookup on every run or encode knowledge as an agent skill.
